children: By Staff Writer
In Kabizi, a village in Jinja district, a single vegetable plot is being watched more closely than most.

Rows of nakati (African eggplant), dodo (Amaranth), sukuma wiki (kale), cabbage and tomatoes are growing under an unusual arrangement: farmers, researchers and a biological-inputs company have agreed to let the plot answer a question that has been building for years. Can Uganda grow vegetables without poisoning its soil, killing pests’ natural predators or putting consumers at risk? Can farmers earn as much as – or more than – they do by spraying?Pests and diseases account for more than 30 per cent of vegetable yield losses nationally. Farmers have tried to chemically treat their way out of the losses, but returns are diminishing even as fertiliser and pesticide bills rise. Getting ahead of those losses cheaply is the economic pitch behind agroecology. Whether it holds up under real market conditions is what the plot in Kabizi has to prove.“We noticed that we need to take technology out from research to the field,” said Dr Joshua Okonya, a programme officer at ASARECA, a regional agricultural research organisation.“Adoption has been low for these technologies. Why? Maybe because we involve fewer farmers.”The living-lab model is designed to close that gap by making farmers co-designers rather than an audience. They will run the plots themselves, tracking pest pressure and crop growth against a conventionally managed comparison plot, while partners check in monthly over the next four to six months.

The pressure they are up against is impatience.“We moved from how agriculture came into existence to how we became impatient and want food to grow very fast,” said Kambaire Justine Kizza, a programme officer in PELUM Uganda’s agroecology department.

That impatience, she said, has driven heavier chemical use across the country. “Most farmers are using reckless methods – unsafe, highly hazardous pesticides, highly synthetic fertiliser that affect the soils,” Kizza added.
Her argument is that degraded soil produces weaker crops, which become more vulnerable to pests and disease, creating a cycle in which farmers reach for more chemicals while the problem remains.

For Ivan Arinda, a consultant at Koppert, a biological crop protection and natural pollination firm, the fix starts underground. Farmers increasingly cultivate the same plots season after season, continuously depleting the soil.“Good soil health guarantees good production. The plant is stable; it grows vigorously, even faster than the pest can develop,” he said.

His approach is not to abandon chemicals, but to change the order: prevention first, biological control next, synthetic intervention only when necessary. “We don’t start from the problem. We start from the preparation, prevention, control,” he said.
What that looks like beyond a demonstration plot is visible a short distance from Kabizi, at Ksam Farm, an agroecological site run by farmer-trainer Samuel Kabuye.
Residue from black soldier fly larvae helps control insects attacking vegetables. Jack beans, planted as trap crops, draw pests away while fixing nitrogen and helping to regulate soil moisture.

Nutrient-rich water from fish ponds irrigates and fertilises vegetables, bananas and coffee. Instead of buying fertiliser, the farm produces its own, including a preparation called SK-99 for sustaining soil micro-organisms through drought.

For Kabuye, the economics are about stacking small substitutions, each removing another reason to buy a pesticide or fertiliser.“Once the roots become destroyed... it will make the farmer look for a pesticide, yet the problem is the root,” he said.

In Murang’a County, Kenya, the World Vegetable Centre (WorldVeg) Greener Greens project had farmers grow traditional leafy vegetables using intercropping, biological pest control and compost instead of chemical fertiliser.

In a study, WorldVeg says participants reported higher yields, better marketability and fewer post-harvest losses than those who used conventional methods. However, the findings were self-reported from a first-phase pilot.
At national scale, trade data suggests the market for “clean” food is real, and growing faster than production.

Uganda’s National Organic Agriculture Policy estimated that organic exports of coffee, sesame, chia, fruit, vanilla and other high-value crops earned about $50 million in 2018, roughly 17 per cent of agricultural export value that year.

By 2023, that figure had risen to roughly $159 million, while Uganda’s organic agriculture umbrella body, NOGAMU, projected an increase of 40 per cent in 2024. Yet the organisation estimates that only about two per cent of domestic demand for organic produce is being met.
That gap should favour the kind of biological, low-input farming being tested in Kabizi – if farmers can reach those markets and prove what they are selling.

Uganda has no widely recognised national way to signal food was grown without synthetic chemicals, with the instant credibility consumers associate with a Uganda National Bureau of Standards mark.“Agroecology has not yet been popularised. Where is it?” asked Hadijah Nalule, PELUM Uganda’s programme officer.
What exists is fragmented: the Kilimo Hai mark and the government-recognised Participatory Guarantee System, which is community-based rather than nationwide.
At Nakasero, vendors advertise an “organic” section that often means indigenous crop varieties.
In Kampala markets such as Nakawa, “organic” can mean herbal remedies. The problem, Nalule says, is a market that has never been taught the distinction.
